query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy, deformation at intermediate temperatures and high strain rates induces fast nanosegregation of principal constituent elements (e.g., Ni, Cr, Mn) to grain boundaries, thereby reducing cohesion and promoting a transition from ductile transgranular to brittle intergranular fracture that degrades toughness. By contrast, if the alloy is pre-engineered with grain-boundary precipitates that can ‘absorb’ the segregating elements to preserve grain-boundary cohesion, the brittle behavior is suppressed.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or homogenized single-phase high-entropy alloy with a compositionally complex, disordered solid-solution microstructure (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi HEA).
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled pre-existing grain-boundary second-phase (e.g., Cr-rich precipitates) by a tailored heat treatment or minor alloying (segregation engineering) designed to trap embrittling elements away from the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Tensile or creep testing at intermediate to high service temperatures and at strain rates that promote significant dislocation activity. The comparison involves samples that are otherwise identical except for the controlled presence or absence of preexisting grain-boundary precipitates.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary composition and cohesion modified by either deformation-induced nanosegregation of principal elements or by pre-established precipitates that act as sinks for these elements.
generation.mechanism: Under mechanical loading (at elevated temperature and/or high strain rate), mobile dislocations drive a rapid local migration of principal elements to the grain boundaries, leading to nanosegregation that impairs cohesion and promotes intergranular cracking in the unmodified HEA; preexisting precipitates, however, preferentially absorb these elements, preserving grain-boundary integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Unmodified single-phase HEA samples will exhibit a reduction in toughness (exhibited by brittle intergranular fracture features) relative to the engineered samples. In the engineered sample with grain-boundary precipitates, segregation of embrittling elements will be reduced at the boundaries, maintaining a higher ductility and toughness under the same service conditions.
generation.baseline: The initial state is a homogeneous, single-phase HEA with no engineered grain-boundary precipitates and known favorable strength–ductility combinations at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under service conditions involving intermediate temperatures (e.g., 500–700°C) and strain rates that promote dislocation motion – conditions not typically leading to rapid grain coarsening or intermetallic formation in HEAs.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of the segregation process and its sensitivity to specific alloy compositions and processing histories remain uncertain. Additionally, the quantitative impact of preexisting precipitates on altering the segregation dynamics needs further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples with identical bulk compositions. One set remains as a single-phase material (control) while the other undergoes a controlled heat treatment to introduce preexisting, Cr-rich grain-boundary precipitates. Subject both sets to tensile (or creep) tests at intermediate temperatures (500–700°C) and comparable strain rates. Simultaneously, perform atom probe tomography (APT) or similar high-resolution analyses to quantify elemental segregation at grain boundaries post-deformation.
measurements: Fracture surface analysis (SEM/TEM) to identify intergranular vs. transgranular fracture modes
Mechanical property curves (stress-strain) to assess toughness and ductility
APT measurements quantifying the degree of principal-element segregation at grain boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the control and precipitate-engineered samples exhibit similar levels of grain-boundary nanosegregation of principal elements and identical brittle intergranular fracture features (i.e., similar loss of toughness), then the hypothesis that grain-boundary segregation governs toughness degradation in the single-phase HEA is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: During the tensile test process at intermediate temperatures in the air, intermetallic phases were not yet formed in coarse-grained Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni HEAs, owing to a short testing time (a few minutes). In addition, the above-mentioned oxide and hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms can be ruled out because these alloys show good resistance to oxidation at intermediate temperatures and hydrogen embrittlement at relatively low hydrogen concentrations (, ). These facts suggest that temperature-induced ductility loss in fcc-phase HEAs/MEAs could be related to segregation of some of the principal elements during the short testing time, which causes GB decohesion. We examined this hypothesis in an equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA and revealed the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni separately into GBs, which accounts for ductility loss with increasing temperature. Correspondingly, we proposed and demonstrated that preexisting precipitates can migrate the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni into the precipitates instead of at GBs, which can effectively evade ductility loss during deformation at intermediate temperatures.

cited_evidence.text: To evade the fast segregation of principal elements Ni, Cr, and Mn into GBs, we propose to migrate the fast segregation of these elements from GBs to the preexisting precipitates that are enriched with principal embrittling elements, especially for alloys used at intermediate and high temperatures, because intermetallic compounds can deform at high temperatures, although they reduce the ductility of the alloys at room temperature compared with the single-phase alloys. On the basis of the chemical compositions of four possible GB precipitates in the Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA reported by previous studies (see table S1) (, , ), the Cr-rich σ phase absorbs Cr elements, while it repels other element segregation to GBs. Otto et al. found that GBs are rich in Ni and have no obvious segregation of embrittling elements Mn and Cr when Cr-rich σ phases were precipitated at GBs (, ). In addition, without Mn, Ni segregated in σ phase–free GBs is beneficial to GB cohesion. cited_evidence.text: Although the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is lower than the single-phase HEA at the testing temperature below 500°C, the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is greater than the single-phase HEA at 600° and 700°C. No intergranular embrittlement is observed. Figure 5 (B and C) shows the lateral surface in the vicinity of the fracture after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. Figure 5 (D and E) exhibits typical ductile dimples on fracture surfaces after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. In contrast to single-phase samples (Fig. 3D), the dual-phase sample has very few cracks near the lateral fracture surface. This suggests that the GB segregation engineering strategy via preexisting Cr-rich precipitates is effective to evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures in HEAs. This is because the embrittling elements—such as Cr, Mn, or Ni—can be absorbed by preexisting embrittling element–enriched precipitates at GBs, which only leads to the growth of precipitates rather than GB embrittlement.
